name: to_static_string
workload: Converting long integers and doubles to strings via Google Benchmark, comparing std::to_string, to_static_string, and std::to_chars.
claimed_speedup: std::to_string(long) 45.3ns vs to_static_string(long) 27.7ns vs std::to_chars(long) 27.4ns; std::to_string(double) 1245ns vs to_static_string(double) 95.6ns vs std::to_chars(double) 98.4ns (numbers verbatim from README table; ~1.6x and ~13x ratios are derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: clang-18, CMake Release build configuration; exact -O flags not individually quoted on the page
tradeoffs: Header-only and narrowly scoped to numeric-to-string conversion (not a general string/container replacement); non-allocating and non-throwing by design but feature surface is much smaller than std::string; very low adoption so far.
caveats: Single-author project with only 1 star and a single benchmark machine (a laptop-class CPU); README itself says 'testing is still an ongoing effort'; no independent reproduction found.

name: StringZilla
workload: Substring search (5-byte random word) and line-splitting throughput over large text buffers (GB/s), and ~100-byte DNA Levenshtein edit-distance throughput (MCUPS), on two machines.
claimed_speedup: Substring search: STL std::string::find 9.1 GB/s vs StringZilla sz_find 21.0 GB/s on Xeon4 (~2.3x, derived from page data); std::string::find 10.9 GB/s vs sz_find 37.1 GB/s on Apple M5 Pro (~3.4x, derived from page data); line splitting: libc strcspn 9.2 GB/s vs StringZilla 13.8 GB/s (Xeon4) and 3.8 vs 23.7 GB/s (M5 Pro) (numbers verbatim from README table)
compiler_and_flags: GCC/glibc on Xeon4; Apple clang/libc++ on M5 Pro; exact optimization flags (e.g. -O3/-march) not stated in the README/CONTRIBUTING text reviewed
hardware: Intel Xeon 4th-gen Sapphire Rapids ('Xeon4'); Apple M5 Pro (18-core Apple Silicon)
tradeoffs: Large SIMD/SWAR codebase targeting many backends (AVX2/AVX-512/SVE/NEON, GPU) and languages; C++ wrapper layered on a C core, so API surface differs from plain std::string in places; peak gains are hardware-dependent (results vary substantially between the two tested machines).
caveats: This is the project's own first-party benchmark suite; exact compiler flags used for the published numbers are not stated in the pages reviewed, so per methodology rules this is capped at Tier C despite public benchmark code and a stated CPU model.

name: Str (MengRao/str)
workload: Fixed-length string equality/comparison microbenchmarks, and integer/float parsing and formatting (fromi/toi) microbenchmarks, in the project's own bundled benchmark.
claimed_speedup: "2x faster than strncmp/memcmp or those of std::string" (comparisons); "10x faster than stoi/strtol/to_string/sprintf" (integer/float conversions) (verbatim from README)
tradeoffs: Str is a fixed maximum-length string type (template-parameterized capacity), not a resizable/dynamic string like std::string, so it is not a drop-in replacement; also ships an adaptive open-addressing hash table (StrHash) claiming 7x over std::unordered_map, which is out of scope for this category but shows the project's low-latency/trading-oriented design focus.
caveats: No compiler, flags, or hardware stated for the quoted 2x/10x numbers; repo has had no commits since 2021 (>5 years), so treat as unmaintained; numbers are first-party and unverified independently.

name: FastString
workload: Constructing small (fixed-capacity, stack-allocated) and large strings from const char*/buffer, and append operations, measured with Google Benchmark.
claimed_speedup: From const char: std::string 498ns vs FastString 46.9ns (~10.6x, derived from page data); large string construction: 1048ns vs 153ns (~6.8x, derived); append: 190ns vs 164ns (~1.2x, derived); append (large): 50.0ns vs 61.5ns (FastString ~0.8x, i.e. slightly slower, derived) (raw ns numbers verbatim from README table)
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 19.28.29334.0 (VS2019); also mentions testing with x86-64 gcc-trunk but that results table was not shown on the page; exact optimization flags not stated
hardware: Reported only as "8 x 1498 MHz CPU" (Google Benchmark auto-detected core count/clock) with L1d 48KiB x4, L1i 32KiB x4, L2 512KiB x4, L3 8192KiB — no explicit CPU model name given
tradeoffs: Fixed-size, stack-allocated string with a compile-time capacity template parameter; cannot grow beyond that capacity, so it is not a general-purpose std::string replacement; the project's own numbers show append-heavy workloads can be at parity or slightly slower than std::string.
caveats: Hardware is reported only as core-count and clock frequency (no CPU model name), so per methodology rules this is capped at Tier C rather than A even though a compiler version and code are given.

name: zuu_string_view
workload: find_first_of, find (substring), rfind (substring), and find (char) operations over string_view-like objects, measured with Google Benchmark.
claimed_speedup: find_first_of: std::string_view 15.7ns vs zuu_string_view 6.11ns (~2.5x, derived from page data); find (substring): 14.1ns vs 11.1ns (~1.3x, derived); rfind: 16.7ns vs 11.4ns (~1.4x, derived); find (char): 2.24ns vs 1.56ns (~1.4x, derived) (raw ns numbers verbatim from README table)
hardware: Reported only as "12 x 2096 MHz CPU" (Google Benchmark auto-detected core count/clock) — no explicit CPU model name given
tradeoffs: Still a non-owning view like std::string_view, so offers no lifetime-safety improvement; C++11-compatible target may limit some modern-compiler optimizations available to libc++/libstdc++; extremely small/early codebase (31 commits) with minimal external validation.
caveats: No LICENSE file found (usability tagged 'reference', not 'copyable'); 0 stars, very early-stage project; compiler and optimization flags not stated; hardware given only as core count/clock, not a model name.

name: jank persistent_string
workload: Small/medium string allocation, copy-construction, find, substring-extraction, and equality-comparison microbenchmarks (nanobench) comparing jank's persistent_string to std::string and folly::fbstring.
claimed_speedup: Blog states persistent_string "ties or outperforms the fastest" of std::string/folly::fbstring across every benchmark shown, and is fastest at constructing small strings; results are presented only as bar charts on the page, with no exact numeric values stated in the surrounding text
tradeoffs: persistent_string is an immutable, reference-counted/shared string tied to jank's own runtime and GC model (copy-on-substring semantics, writes only in constructors); it is not a standalone drop-in std::string replacement usable outside jank's runtime without adopting that model.
caveats: No exact numbers could be extracted (results shown only as chart images on the blog; the linked nanobench gist contains only the benchmark harness/setup code, not executed results), so this is capped at Tier D per the rules; included only because the project is clearly notable (3.3k+ stars) and the claim is specific and on-topic.
